questions.q: In the dcp.load example, why is the model built with build_model() before dcp.load is called, rather than loading state directly into nothing?
options: dcp.load needs an existing model/optimizer state_dict structure to know where each loaded shard belongs
Building the model first is purely optional and has no functional purpose
PyTorch requires models to be built twice for every training run
It is required only for single-GPU training, not distributed training
questions.explain: dcp.load fills in an existing state_dict structure with the matching shard data from the checkpoint, so the model and optimizer must already be constructed (with the right shapes) before loading.

questions.q: What key capability does DCP's sharded, metadata-based checkpoint have that a plain torch.save checkpoint does not?
options: It can be loaded back onto a different number of GPUs/ranks than the run that saved it, by resharding according to the metadata
It saves files that are always smaller than a torch.save checkpoint
It automatically encrypts the checkpoint at rest
It eliminates the need for an optimizer state entirely
questions.explain: Because DCP's checkpoint includes metadata describing shard boundaries rather than being tied to a fixed device layout, it can be reshard-loaded onto a different world size — something a plain torch.save checkpoint, tied to its original layout, cannot do.

questions.q: Why does the launch script check that a checkpoint's metadata is 'complete' before loading it, rather than just loading the most recent checkpoint prefix?
options: Completeness checks are unnecessary busywork with no real risk otherwise
A checkpoint interrupted by the very failure being recovered from might be only partially written, so loading it directly could fail or load corrupt/inconsistent state
S3 automatically deletes incomplete checkpoints, so this check is redundant
It is required by AWS billing policy for S3 buckets
questions.explain: If the failure that triggered the resume happened during a checkpoint write, the most recent checkpoint could be incomplete. Verifying completeness before loading avoids resuming from a corrupt or partial save.

questions.q: Why is 'the job resumed without throwing an exception' not sufficient proof that the resume was correct?
options: Exceptions are disabled in distributed PyTorch jobs

A clean load only proves the checkpoint files were readable — it doesn't confirm the optimizer state, learning-rate schedule position, or step count are actually consistent with where training left off, which a loss-continuity check verifies
PyTorch always throws an exception on successful resume, so no exception means failure
Exceptions only ever indicate hardware failures, never software issues
questions.explain: Successfully reading the checkpoint files is a much weaker guarantee than training actually resuming in a consistent state. Watching whether loss tracks smoothly from the resume point catches subtler mismatches that a successful file load wouldn't.

questions.q: A replacement PyTorchJob after a node failure launches with 60 nodes instead of the original 64. What does dcp.load do in this situation?
options: It fails outright, because checkpoints can only be loaded onto the exact world size that saved them
It reshards the saved checkpoint state across the new 60-node world size using the checkpoint's metadata
It silently drops 4 nodes' worth of model weights, corrupting the model
It pads the checkpoint with random weights to fill the missing capacity
questions.explain: DCP's checkpoint isn't tied to a fixed rank layout. Its metadata lets dcp.load redraw shard boundaries to fit whatever world size the new job actually launches with, including a smaller one.
